**Polished Version:**

When you don the mask, the thunder begins. Through the nostril's orange glow, you can smell the distant hope of rain. High in the Nilgiris, the eucalyptus glistens, the pine trees drip, and spiders tumble from their silver webs. The mask lies raw and red as bark against the bones of your face. You trace the stripes, ridged like the old welts of your childhood. A wind is rising in the north, and a scarlet light glows like fire across the sky.

When you gaze through the eyeholes, it is like falling. Night wraps you in gauze of black. You are as blind as at the dawn of the world. You breathe deep. You seek the moon. In time, you come to know that the creased, musky scent is rising from your own skin.

Once you find the ears, the drums begin. Your fur bristles and stiffens. A roar sounds from the distant left, like the surge of monsoon waters. You swivel your sightless head. Beneath your sheathed paw, the ground shifts, wet and yielding.

What is that small, wild sound sheltering within your skull, set against the circle that always closes in just before the dawn?

**Note:** The poem refers to a ritual performed by certain Rajasthani hill tribes to ensure rain and a bountiful harvest.

As soon as the mask covers your face, the thunder begins. The scent of distant, hopeful rain reaches you through the orange of the nostril. High in the Nilgiris, eucalyptus shimmers, pine trees weep moisture, and spiders drop from their silvery threads. Against your cheekbones, the mask feels rough and crimson, like tree bark. Your fingers trace the stripes, raised like scars remembered from your youth. A breeze builds toward the north, and a red glow fills the heavens like flames.

Peering out through the eyeholes feels like plummeting. Darkness wraps around you like black fabric. You cannot see, just as no one could when the world first began. Breathe in. Hunt for the moon. In time, you'll realize that wrinkled, musky odor comes from your own body. The moment your fingers find the ears, drumming sounds erupt. The hair on your body bristles. Somewhere far to your left comes a roar, resembling the rush of monsoon floods. You turn your unseeing head from side to side. Beneath your covered paw, the earth grows damp and unsteady.

What is that faint, untamed noise hiding within your skull, resisting the ring that always tightens around you in the final moments before daybreak?

Note: This poem describes a ceremony carried out by certain hill tribes in Rajasthan to bring rain and secure an abundant harvest.

The moment the mask settles against the face, a profound sensory transformation begins. It arrives first as thunder—a low, resonant rumble that seems to gather in the body—followed by the anticipated smell of rain, that green and mineral scent which promises the breaking of drought. This is not merely the act of covering one's face; it is the crossing of a threshold into another mode of being.

The mask itself is a living thing in its texture and presence. Raw and red like bark, it carries the roughness of the natural world against the skin. This tactile encounter awakens something deep within the speaker, evoking vivid memories from childhood—sensations long buried but never forgotten, surging back with the immediacy of the first time they were felt.

To look through the mask's eyeholes is to lose one's ordinary bearings. The narrow apertures create a disorienting, blinding sensation, a flood of confusion that strips away the accumulated layers of adult perception. In that moment the wearer is returned to a primal state, cast back to something like the world's beginning, when everything was new and undivided and charged with elemental force.

From this disorientation the transformation deepens. The wearer begins to take on animal characteristics: fur rises across the skin, hands become paws, and the senses sharpen to an uncanny acuity. The ears grow attuned to the pounding of drums and to distant roars carried on the wind—sounds that belong to the wilderness rather than to human society. The boundary between person and creature dissolves, and the wearer inhabits an older, wilder consciousness.

All of this belongs to a ritual performed by certain Rajasthani hill tribes, enacted to ensure the coming of rain and the promise of a bountiful harvest. The poem thus captures not only a personal, bodily metamorphosis but a communal act of faith—an ancient ceremony in which putting on the mask means summoning the powers of the earth and sky to sustain the life of the people.

# The Rain Mask

When they fitted the mask over my face, the world narrowed to two slits of failing light. The carved wood pressed against my cheekbones, still smelling of the cedar oil the elders had rubbed into its grain, and I understood that I would not be myself again until the ritual released me.

At first I fought to see. The hill fell away below us in terraces of dry earth, the crops brittle and waiting, and beyond them the plains shimmered under a sky the color of hammered brass. But the eyeholes were small, deliberately so, and as the drums began their low insistence the visible world contracted until sight seemed the least of my senses—a thing I could set down like a tool no longer needed.

Then came the smell. Earth, first: the particular scent of soil that has thirsted too long, mineral and sharp. Then the animal musk worked into the mask's inner lining, fur and sweat and something older, and I breathed it the way a beast breathes, wide-nostrilled, reading the air for what it promised. Somewhere to the east, though I could not have said how I knew, the atmosphere was changing. The dryness carried an edge now, a dampness gathering at the rim of things.

The sound rose to meet it. The drums were no longer outside me but within, matched to a pulse I no longer recognized as my own heartbeat. Voices circled—the villagers chanting the old syllables that have no meaning anyone remembers, only power—and beneath them, far off, a first low roll of thunder answered like a larger drum struck in the belly of the sky.

I was becoming something else.

I felt the fur at my shoulders as though it grew from me. My spine curved. My hands, when I looked down through the narrow slits, seemed the paws of a creature crouched to spring. The named things fell away one by one: my village name, my father's name, the names of the fields I had walked since childhood. What remained was appetite and instinct, the animal alertness of a body wholly given to anticipation. I waited as the parched land waited. I hungered as the roots hungered. There was no line anymore between the thirst in the soil and the thirst in me.

The thunder came closer. Fur, earth, the electric weight of a coming storm—these were the only truths, and I inhabited them completely, no longer a man wearing a mask but a vessel emptied of self so that something older could pour through. This, I understood in the wordless place where understanding now lived, was the meaning of the ceremony: not that we ask the rain to come, but that we cease, for a time, to be separate from it. We dissolve the boundary. We become the elemental thing we plead with.

And so we danced through the darkest hours, the circle turning, the drums and thunder braided into one voice, until the sky finally broke and the first fat drops struck the mask and ran down its carved cheeks like the tears of a face that could not weep on its own.

By dawn the rain had come in earnest. The circle closed—the dancers drawing inward, shoulder to shoulder, the ritual folding back on itself as the sun rose gray and streaming behind the clouds. Slowly, the mask grew heavy again. Slowly, sight returned, and sound became only sound, and I felt my own name settle back over me like a wet garment.

They lifted the mask away. My face was raw where the wood had pressed, tender and exposed to the cold morning air. I stood among the others, human again, small again, trembling with a vulnerability I had not felt before I surrendered myself—as though in becoming the storm I had learned, at last, how fragile it is to be only a man, standing in a field, grateful for the water falling on the harvest.

# A Journey Through the Nilgiris

**When** you first set eyes upon the Nilgiris, you understand at once why they are called the "Blue Mountains." A soft, misty haze drapes itself across the rolling hills, giving the entire landscape a serene bluish tint that seems almost otherworldly. Located in the Western Ghats of southern India, this region has captivated travelers, poets, and nature lovers for generations.

Traveling **through** the Nilgiris is an experience that engages every sense. The winding mountain roads climb steadily upward, revealing sweeping vistas of terraced tea plantations that stretch as far as the eye can see. The famous Nilgiri Mountain Railway, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, chugs slowly through tunnels and past waterfalls, carrying passengers on one of the most scenic journeys in the country. As you pass **through** dense forests and open grasslands, you may glimpse wild elephants, gaur, and countless species of birds that call these hills home.

**When** the cool highland air fills your lungs, the stresses of everyday life seem to melt away. Towns like Ooty, Coonoor, and Kotagiri offer charming reminders of the region's colonial past, with their old bungalows, botanical gardens, and bustling local markets fragrant with fresh spices and eucalyptus.

Ultimately, a trip **through** the Nilgiris is not merely a destination—it is a passage into tranquility. **When** you finally leave, you carry with you memories of misty mornings, endless green slopes, and the quiet majesty of the Blue Mountains.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about someone putting on a ritual animal mask and transforming, set in the Nilgiri hills of India, with sensory imagery of rain, fur, and drums. Add a note explaining it refers to a Rajasthani rain ritual.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Wearing

Rain comes to the Nilgiri hills like a language remembered—first a whisper against the shola leaves, then a downpour that fills the mouth of every ravine. She waits at the threshold where the drums have already begun, their skins tightened by the wet until each beat lands low in the belly, a second pulse beneath her own.

The mask is heavier than she expected. Fur, coarse and dark, still smelling of animal and woodsmoke and the oil rubbed into it by hands older than her grandmother's. She lifts it. For a moment the world narrows to the eyeholes, to the breath trapped hot against her cheeks, to the weight settling on her skull like a crown of another kingdom.

Then the drums find her ribs and she is no longer only herself.

The fur becomes her fur. The rain that streams from the mask's snout is rain from her own muzzle now. She feels the forest lean toward her—the leech and the langur, the mist braiding through the eucalyptus, the red earth turning to appetite beneath the storm. Something four-legged wakes inside the human cage of her hips. She stamps. The gathered ones answer with their throats.

She is the hunger the rains must feed. She is the beast the sky agreed to answer. When she dances, the water dances. When she bows her heavy head, the clouds bow theirs, and the whole green world drinks.

---

*Note: This poem draws loosely on Rajasthani rain-invocation traditions, in which ritual performance—song, drumming, and the wearing of animal or deity guises—is enacted to summon the monsoon during periods of drought. In such rites, the performer is understood not merely to represent a creature or spirit but to become a vessel through which the community petitions the rains. I have transplanted the ritual's spirit to the wetter, mist-heavy landscape of the Nilgiri hills in the south for atmospheric contrast; the geographical pairing is a poetic liberty rather than an ethnographic record.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a second-person poem describing the experience of a shamanic transformation during a tribal rain-and-harvest ceremony, using vivid sensory details and ending with an ambiguous, haunting question.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Turning

You feel the drum before you hear it—
a pulse that climbs the ladder of your spine,
each beat a rung, each rung a leaving.
The fire spits its orange language at your feet.

You taste the smoke of burning sage and something older,
bitter on the root of your tongue,
the ceremonial draught still working
its slow unraveling through your blood.

The elders' voices braid the dark.
You sway. The painted ochre on your chest
begins to breathe, the red lines lifting
like veins that are no longer only yours.

Now the rain arrives—you smell it first,
that mineral hunger rising from the clay,
and when it breaks against your upturned face
you cannot tell your skin from the downpour.

Your hands remember feathers.
Your shoulders ache with the memory of wings
you never had, or always had,
and the corn stalks bow their tasseled heads like kin.

You are the field. You are the flood.
The seed cracks open in your ribcage,
green and desperate, reaching
for a sun that lives behind your eyes.

The world goes liquid at its edges.
You dissolve into the wet percussion,
into the mud that made the first of everyone,
into the roots that drink the sky.

And when you surface—gasping, changed,
the rain still ringing in your marrow—
you look down at these strange familiar hands
and cannot say what crossed the water in your place:

*Who wears your body now,
and where has the one who entered gone?*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical piece where wearing a mask causes the narrator to become a wild animal, blending Indian landscape imagery with themes of blindness, ritual, and dawn.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Mask at First Light

I tied the cloth of tiger-dark across my sleeping eyes,
and where the sun should split the neem, I felt my knuckles rise—
not hands now, but the padded weight of something meant to prowl,
the river of my human name dissolved into a growl.

*Blind, blind,* the mask had made me blind,
yet sharper grew the world:
the smell of cardamom and dust, of jasmine tightly curled,
the temple bells like distant birds across the paddy green,
and I, a beast, unseeing, saw what eyes have never seen.

The dawn came bleeding through the palms, a saffron-colored rite,
and priests I could not witness poured their offerings to light.
The banyan spread its hundred arms, each root a knotted prayer,
while I stole low through elephant grass and breathed the burning air.

What ritual is this, that fur should grow where flesh had lain?
The Ganges of my former self runs backward, cool as rain—
I am the thing the villagers once whispered by the fire,
the yellow eye in monsoon dark, the shape of old desire.

*Blind, blind,* and yet I am the seer,
the mask my only truth—
I shed the man like cotton robes, the softness of my youth,
and pad toward the reddening east where dawn and hunger meet,
my shadow long across the fields, four wild and silent feet.

When sun stands whole above the hills, will I put off the face?
Or has the tiger swallowed me, this blindness now my grace?
The marigolds are opening. The morning drums begin.
I lift my muzzle to the light—and let the wildness in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an evocative prose poem in the style of Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni about a rain ritual mask, then include a short explanatory note about its cultural origin.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Rain Mask Speaks

I am carved from the wood of the tree that drinks deepest, the one whose roots remember every monsoon before you were born, before your grandmother's grandmother pressed her wet feet into this same red earth.

They painted my cheeks with turmeric and the ash of seven fires. My eyes are hollow so the sky can see through them—so the clouds mistake me for their own lost child and come weeping home.

Feel how the drummers wake me. Feel how the women circle, their anklets speaking the language of small thunders, their voices climbing the humid air like vines seeking something to hold. I have swallowed a hundred dry seasons. I have tasted the cracked lips of the fields, the way the wells go silent, the way the buffalo stand with their heads bowed low as mourners.

Wear me, and you are no longer the potter's son, no longer the girl who sweeps the temple steps. Wear me, and you become the throat through which the village begs. Wear me, and the first fat drop will land upon my painted brow like a blessing, like a coin dropped into the palm of the patient poor.

Afterward, they will hang me in the rafters where the smoke can keep me. I will listen to the rain I called, drumming its long fingers on the thatch, and I will dream in the dark of my next thirst, my next dance, the next parched mouth that needs a face to speak its wanting to the merciless and merciful heavens.

---

**A Note on Origin**

Rain ritual masks appear across many agrarian cultures where survival depends on the timely arrival of seasonal rains. In parts of rural India, Southeast Asia, and West Africa, communities have long employed carved masks in ceremonial dances meant to invoke the monsoon or end a drought. Such masks are typically fashioned from local wood and adorned with natural pigments—turmeric, ash, ochre—each carrying symbolic weight. The dancer who dons the mask is understood to become a vessel or intermediary, temporarily setting aside individual identity to embody a communal plea to the divine. After the ceremony, masks are often stored in the smoke of household hearths, both to preserve the wood against insects and to honor their sacred function until they are called upon again. This poem is an imaginative work rather than a depiction of one specific tradition.

counterfactuals.output:
# The Rain That Wears a Face

You press the mask against your face and the world exhales.

The clay is cool, then warm, then something that is neither—it becomes your second skin, and you feel the painted spirals across your cheeks begin to turn, slow as galaxies. You cannot see your own eyes anymore. You are looking out through holes that belong to someone older than you, someone who was dancing before you were born and will be dancing after you dissolve.

The drums are underground. You feel them in the soles of your feet before you hear them, a heartbeat that the earth borrowed and forgot to return. You begin to move, though you did not decide to. Your knees remember steps your mind never learned.

Around you, the others are becoming their masks too. The one with the heron's beak. The one whose face is a black sun. You know their names in daylight, but daylight is a country you have left. Now they are only the shapes the sky is waiting for.

You lift your arms and the clouds notice.

This is the part you will never be able to explain: how the sweat on your spine turns to a colder wetness, how you cannot tell if it is your body weeping or the first fat drop landing between your shoulders. You dance harder. The mask grows heavier, drinking, drinking. Thunder answers the drums like an older brother finally coming home.

And when the rain arrives—when it truly arrives, silvering the dust, filling the cracked mouths of the fields—you understand that you did not summon it.

You *became* the invitation.

You lower the mask. The spirals stop turning. You are only yourself again, soaked and small, laughing without knowing why, while the water writes its long-awaited letter across the thirsty ground.

---

**A Factual Note**

Rain-summoning rituals involving masks appear across many cultures, though the surreal passage above is an imaginative composite rather than a depiction of any single tradition. Among the **Hopi** people of the American Southwest, *Katsina* (Kachina) ceremonies feature masked dancers who embody spirit beings believed to bring rain and agricultural fertility to an arid landscape; the masks are treated as sacred, and the wearer is understood to take on the spirit's presence. Similar rain-oriented masked and dance traditions exist among various West African peoples, the Indigenous nations of the Andes, and Aboriginal Australian communities. Anthropologists generally interpret such rituals as expressions of a reciprocal relationship between a community and the natural forces it depends upon—acts of participation and petition rather than mere spectacle. Because many of these ceremonies remain living, sacred practices, their specific details are often protected and not shared publicly.
